summary: Two corpora: Šuruppak administration and the Abu Ṣalābīḫ school; both are small.
Girsu is one household over c. 20 years; Umma, Adab and Nippur are smaller groups.
Everything comes from one palace over 40-50 years.
Several provincial households (Girsu, Adab, Umma, Nippur), each one circle of documentation (Foster 1982).
c. 120,000 texts, almost all from provincial and royal archives; most were looted and have no find context (Molina 2016).
No survey separates the early OB sites; our early sample is Nippur, Nērebtum and Tuttul.
More than 50,000 archival texts from c. 60 sites; family archives appear for the first time, and institutional archives cover short spans (Charpin 2014).
c. 22,300 tablets, almost all from c. 40 merchant houses at Kaneš; Assur itself is not documented.
c. 12,000 texts from Nippur, mostly unpublished, against a few hundred elsewhere.
Mostly Assur and Kār-Tukultī-Ninurta; perhaps 10% of Assur excavated; provinces under 1,500 texts in all.
c. 25,000 pieces from Nineveh; provincial archives are counted in dozens (Fales 2021).
c. 19,000 texts; more than half from the Eanna and Ebabbar temples; no royal archive survives (Jursa 2010).
Persepolis Fortification (c. 13,000 tablets) and Treasury; in Babylonia, a sharp drop after 484 to c. 2,000 texts, mostly Murašû and Kasr.
At least 5,000 texts, written only by temple staff and notables; most records were in Greek or Aramaic on perishable media (Monerie 2018).
c. 30,000 fragments, nearly all from Ḫattuša; provincial finds show the capital kept writing to itself (van den Hout 2020).
c. 400 texts from Haft Tepe (ME I) and 246 from Malyan (end of the period); ME II-III have only royal inscriptions.
